title: Two answers to 'how does 2^ω(n) generalize?'
content: The parent proves ZMod n has 2^ω(n) idempotents (automorphic residues e²≡e mod n). This file answers the parent's open question — how does the count generalize beyond ℤ? — arithmetically and algebraically. Arithmetically, 2^ω(n) is the number of squarefree divisors of n, since squarefree divisors are indexed by subsets of the prime-factor set. Algebraically, the count is a power of two because the Chinese Remainder Theorem writes the modulus as a finite product of LOCAL rings, and a local ring has only the trivial idempotents 0 and 1; this holds equally for ZMod n (factors ZMod pᵏ) and for 𝒪_K/𝔞 (factors 𝒪_K/𝔭ᵏ), the number-ring case named in the open question.
mathContext: $\#\{\text{idempotents of } \mathbb{Z}/n\} = \#\{\text{squarefree divisors of } n\} = 2^{\omega(n)}$, and more generally $2^{(\text{number of local factors})}$ for any CRT product of local rings.

title: Squarefree divisors as the image of the prime-factor powerset
content: squarefreeDivisors n is the finset {d ∈ n.divisors | Squarefree d}. The core geometric fact is that the map s ↦ ∏ p∈s p sends the powerset of n.primeFactors bijectively onto the squarefree divisors: a product of a subset of distinct primes divides n (Nat.prod_primeFactors_dvd) and is squarefree (distinct primes are pairwise coprime, so Finset.squarefree_prod_of_pairwise_isCoprime applies), every squarefree divisor is the product over its own prime factors (Nat.prod_primeFactors_of_squarefree), and the map is injective on the powerset because primeFactors is a left inverse on sets of primes (Nat.primeFactors_prod).
mathContext: $\{\text{squarefree divisors of } n\} = \{\textstyle\prod_{p\in s} p : s \subseteq \text{primeFactors}(n)\}$, a bijection with the powerset.

title: 2^ω(n) squarefree divisors, and the bridge to automorphic residues
content: squarefreeDivisors_card applies Finset.card_image_of_injOn to the powerset bijection and Finset.card_powerset to conclude the number of squarefree divisors is 2^ω(n). idempotents_eq_squarefreeDivisors composes this with the parent's idempotent_count to show the automorphic residues of n are equinumerous with its squarefree divisors. The degenerate cases are pinned down: the count is 1 iff n=1, it is 2 iff n is a prime power, and squarefreeDivisors_ten_pow_card recovers the classical decimal '4' for the modulus 10^k.
mathContext: $\#\{\text{squarefree divisors of } n\} = 2^{\omega(n)}$, and $\#\{e : e^2=e \bmod n\} = \#\{\text{squarefree divisors of } n\}$.

title: A local ring has only the idempotents 0 and 1
content: isIdempotentElem_iff_eq_zero_or_one_of_isLocalRing is the crux of the algebraic mechanism. For an idempotent e we have e·(1−e)=0. In a local ring IsLocalRing.isUnit_or_isUnit_one_sub_self makes one of e, 1−e a unit; a unit annihilating its partner forces the partner to be 0, so e=1 or e=0. Since the idempotent subtype is then the two-element set {0,1} (0≠1 in a nontrivial ring), idempotent_count_local gives that a nontrivial local ring has exactly 2 idempotents — the per-factor building block of the product count.
mathContext: $R$ local $\implies (e^2=e \iff e=0 \lor e=1)$; hence a nontrivial local ring has exactly two idempotents.

title: The count 2^(number of local factors), transported across CRT
content: isIdempotentElem_pi_iff records that idempotents of a product ring are exactly the coordinatewise idempotents. Composing Equiv.subtypeEquivRight and Equiv.subtypePiEquivPi gives {idempotents of ∏ Rᵢ} ≃ (∀ i, {idempotents of Rᵢ}), so Nat.card_pi and the per-factor count 2 yield idempotent_count_pi_local = 2^(card ι). Finally idempotent_count_of_ringEquiv transports the count across any ring isomorphism S ≃+* ∏ Rᵢ (idempotents correspond under a ring iso via map_mul and injectivity). This is the form the open question needs: CRT provides S ≃+* ∏ Rᵢ for S = ZMod n (factors ZMod pᵢᵏ) and S = 𝒪_K/𝔞 (factors 𝒪_K/𝔭ᵢᵏ), so each count is 2^(number of distinct primes).
mathContext: $\text{Nat.card}\,\{e \in \textstyle\prod_i R_i : e^2=e\} = 2^{|\iota|}$, and the same for any $S \cong \prod_i R_i$.
